Conformal Uncertainty Quantification
for Mammographic Malignancy Classification

Knowing When the Model Doesn’t Know
PROJECT 8 · DISEASE MODELLING
DenseNet-121 · CBIS-DDSM
ACM 40960 · UCD · 2026
Supervisor: Dr. Sarp Akçay Dataset: CBIS-DDSM — 3,568 biopsy-confirmed mammograms Method: Split conformal prediction (LAC / APS / RAPS + Mondrian) Coverage target: α = 0.05 → 95 % guarantee
A DenseNet-121 mammography classifier is wrapped with split conformal prediction — turning uncalibrated scores into label sets guaranteed to contain the true diagnosis 95 % of the time, automatically flagging ambiguous cases for radiologist review.
I

Introduction

Breast cancer is one of the most prevalent cancers worldwide. Mammographic screening is the primary early-detection tool, but radiological interpretation is time-consuming, error-prone, and subject to inter-observer variability.

Deep learning classifiers have shown strong performance on medical-image tasks, yet they have a critical weakness in clinical deployment: they output a single label with an overconfident probability, providing no principled signal of when the prediction should be distrusted.

This project addresses that gap directly. We train a standard DenseNet-121 classifier on biopsy-confirmed mammograms and wrap it with split conformal prediction — a post-hoc uncertainty quantification method that converts raw classifier scores into prediction sets with a distribution-free coverage guarantee, requiring no assumptions on the data distribution or model architecture.

II

The Problem

Our classifier’s raw confidence is off by ECE = 0.205 — a 20-point gap between stated confidence and actual accuracy. This overconfidence is a property of softmax networks generally, not a flaw in this particular model.

What screening actually needs: predictions with a stated, guaranteed error rate — not a number that merely looks like a probability. A confidently wrong “benign” is a missed cancer.
The coverage guarantee (conformal prediction) Pr( Ytrue ∈ C(X) ) ≥ 1 − α  (α = 0.05 here)

When the prediction set contains one label, the model is confident and the case can be auto-reported. When it contains both labels, the model is honestly flagging ambiguity — that case routes to a radiologist.

III

Approach & Pipeline

Backbone: DenseNet-121 pretrained on ImageNet, fine-tuned on CBIS-DDSM for binary (benign / malignant) classification. All splits are at the patient level to prevent data leakage and preserve the conformal guarantee.

Train1,951
Val352
Calibration595
Test670

The calibration split is unique to conformal prediction: never seen during training, used solely to compute the threshold q̂.

Threshold & set construction q̂ = ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉/n quantile of {1−ptrue,i} on cal set
C(x) = { k : pk(x) ≥ 1 − q̂ }
IV

Three Nonconformity Scores

MethodScore definitionSet sizeSingleton %
LAC1 − ptrue 1.694 ± 0.02730.6 %
APSCumulative sorted mass 1.720 ± 0.02828.0 %
RAPSAPS + set-size penalty 1.714 ± 0.02928.6 %
All three hold ≥ 95 % coverage. LAC is tightest on a binary task — RAPS and APS earn their added complexity only with larger label spaces. Comparing all three rather than asserting one is itself a methodological contribution.
V

Real Mammograms with Prediction Sets

Figure 1. Three test-set mammograms with LAC prediction sets.
Three real cases from the held-out test set illustrate how the system behaves in practice. Left — a clear benign: P(malignant) = 0.00, the set collapses to {Benign} and the case can be auto-reported. Centre — a clear malignant: P(malignant) = 1.00, the set is {Malignant} with full confidence. Right — a genuinely ambiguous case: P(benign) = P(malignant) = 0.50; both labels are included, the system honestly flags it for radiologist review. The true label is Malignant — this is the case that must not be auto-reported.
VI

Why Our Numbers Are Trustworthy

Before touching any mammogram, all three conformal methods were validated on synthetic data with known statistics across 200 independent trials at K = 2 and K = 5.

LAC K=20.951 ✓
APS K=20.955 ✓
RAPS K=20.953 ✓

This separates a correct implementation from a fortunate result: the guarantee is not an accident of one dataset. Full code, notebook, and verification script are available in the repository.

References: Angelopoulos & Bates (2021) · Romano, Sesia & Candès (2020) · Angelopoulos et al. (2021, RAPS) · Sadinle et al. (2019, LAC) · Sawyer-Lee et al. (2016, CBIS-DDSM)
VII

Results

Base classifier (DenseNet-121, single-view, 12 epochs): val accuracy 0.733 · test accuracy 0.643 · AUC 0.708. Single-view CBIS-DDSM is genuinely hard; the uncertainty layer is the contribution, not raw accuracy.

Figure 2. Coverage distributions and average set sizes across 100 resamples.
Left panel shows the empirical coverage distribution across 100 independent calibration/test resamples. All three methods cluster tightly around the 0.95 target line (dashed), confirming the guarantee holds empirically — not just on a single lucky split. Right panel shows average prediction-set size: LAC (teal) achieves the smallest sets (1.694), meaning it resolves the most cases to a single confident label. This is the expected result for a binary task and validates the method selection.
Figure 3. Reliability diagram (ECE = 0.205).
Each bar shows observed accuracy vs predicted confidence for a bin of test samples (count shown above). Bars below the dashed diagonal mean the model is over-confident: it claims more certainty than it earns. ECE = 0.205 quantifies this gap. This overconfidence is precisely why raw softmax scores cannot be used directly — and why conformal prediction is necessary.
Figure 4. Clinical decision curve: singleton rate vs α.
As α increases (looser guarantee), more cases resolve to one label (blue, left axis) but empirical coverage falls (orange, right axis). At the operating point α = 0.05 (dotted line): 42 % of cases are auto-resolved at 99 % coverage. This curve is the tool a clinical team would use to choose their operating point.
VIII

Class-Conditional Coverage: the Fix

Figure 5. Marginal vs Mondrian per-class coverage.
Red bars (Marginal): standard split conformal holds 95 % overall but under-covers malignant at 0.893 — meaning 11 % of true cancers fall outside the prediction set. In screening, this is the most dangerous failure mode. Teal bars (Mondrian): calibrating a separate threshold per class restores malignant coverage to 0.960. Mondrian conformal achieves per-class guarantees by construction, at the cost of using only the per-class calibration count. With 595 calibration points across two classes, the estimate is stable.
Key clinical finding: marginal conformal is insufficient in imbalanced screening settings. Mondrian conformal is the correct tool when per-class safety guarantees are required.
IX

Conclusions

  • The guarantee holds empirically. All three methods achieve ≥ 95 % coverage across 100 resamples, verified independently on synthetic data before any real data was used — a correct implementation, not a fortunate result.
  • LAC is most efficient on a binary task (1.694 vs 1.720/1.714), reproducing the theoretical prediction that RAPS earns its complexity only with large label spaces.
  • Marginal conformal under-covers malignant (0.893). Mondrian per-class calibration restores it to 0.960. This is a clinical finding, not an academic one.
  • ECE 0.205 provides concrete motivation for the uncertainty layer: raw softmax confidence cannot be trusted, and the reliability diagram makes this visible.
  • The decision curve turns α from a technical knob into a quantified clinical operating-point choice.
X

Future Work

  • Multi-view bilateral fusion. The architecture (Siamese DenseNet-121 with gated cross-view attention) is designed and implemented; the conformal layer transfers unchanged to its outputs.
  • BI-RADS multi-class grading. The conformal code already handles K > 2 (verified at K = 5); extending to five-class BI-RADS is a one-line label change.
  • Cross-dataset generalisation. Deployment on VinDr-Mammo requires weighted or Mondrian conformal variants to handle distribution shift while preserving the coverage guarantee.
  • Temperature scaling. Reducing the base classifier’s ECE (currently 0.205) before applying conformal prediction would tighten prediction sets further while keeping the guarantee intact.
